title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Shorten combinational division with a shared radix-4 datapath
motivation:
The baseline scores 12.12 iter/sec at only 5.442 MHz. Its reported worst
path takes 199.837 ns through forwarding and the execute ALU, with 156
cells. alu.sv contains separate signed and unsigned divide and remainder
expressions; their combinational division networks are the strongest
candidate for this deep arithmetic path. There are no previous optimization
attempts or recorded lessons for bench. Shortening this datapath can improve
the clock rate for every CoreMark instruction without adding execution cycles.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the real DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU operator expressions inside alu.sv with
one explicitly unrolled, fully combinational unsigned radix-4 restoring
divider, shared by all four operations. This is a local arithmetic mapping
optimization: keep the existing op/a/b/out interface and zero-cycle ALU
latency, so the pipeline and its bus-stall behavior retain their timing.

For signed operations, form 32-bit unsigned operand magnitudes using
two's-complement negation; the magnitude of INT_MIN is 0x80000000.
Precompute zero-extended D, 2D and 3D once at 34-bit width. Unroll sixteen
quotient-digit stages, each consuming the next two dividend bits from MSB
to LSB. Each stage forms a 34-bit trial remainder T = 4*R + next_digit
and computes T-D, T-2D and T-3D IN PARALLEL using 35-bit zero-extended
subtraction. Use the borrow bits to select the largest fitting multiple
and append its two-bit quotient digit; retain the selected remainder for
the next stage. Derive the comparison from each subtraction's borrow,
rather than putting a separate magnitude comparator before a subtractor.
Select mutually exclusive digit candidates with a shallow mux or masked OR;
avoid cascading three subtract-and-test operations within a stage.
Keep wide trial arithmetic explicit to prevent overflow when D >= 2^31.

Obtain both the quotient and remainder from this same network. Apply sign
correction to the quotient using the operand-sign XOR and to the remainder
using the dividend sign. Explicitly override division by zero with quotient
0xffffffff and remainder a, and signed INT_MIN/-1 with quotient 0x80000000
and remainder zero. Select quotient versus remainder by the requested ALU
operation. Preserve every RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS formula exactly and keep the
new real divider outside that substituted formal branch.

The intended gain comes from sixteen serial quotient-digit selections
instead of a conventional thirty-two-row binary divider, with parallel
trial arithmetic and shared signed/unsigned quotient/remainder hardware.
Validate real arithmetic independently of ALTOPS, then use the standard
formal, cosim and Gowin fitness gates. A median Fmax increase above 4.6%
should translate directly into an accepted fitness increase because this
proposal adds no instruction cycles. The main uncertainty is Gowin's
mapping and routing of the parallel subtractors and digit-selection muxes.

changes.description:
Implement the shared sixteen-stage combinational radix-4 divider locally
in this file, with parallel 35-bit trial subtractors, explicit 34-bit
divisor multiples, magnitude conversion, quotient/remainder sign
correction and RV32M exception overrides. Route all four real division
operations through it while preserving the ALTOPS substitutions and
existing ALU interface and latency.

Extend the real DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU checks with deterministic randomized
differential vectors and directed radix-4 digit boundaries near D, 2D
and 3D. Cover all sign combinations, truncation toward zero, unsigned
divisors above 2^31, INT_MIN as either operand, zero divisors, signed
overflow, maximal unsigned operands and consecutive mixed division
operations. Compute signed reference results using integer magnitudes
and explicit sign correction rather than Python floor division.

title: Replace combinational division with a bounded multicycle execute unit
motivation:
The only recorded bench result has median Fmax 5.442 MHz, 12312 LUT4s,
and a 199.837 ns, 156-cell worst path through forwarding and the EX ALU.
alu.sv currently synthesizes signed and unsigned division and remainder
as full combinational / and % expressions selected into the common EX
result. This is a strong candidate for the extreme arithmetic depth:
even ordinary instructions must meet the timing of this shared result
path. The experiment log has no earlier structural attempts, and no
LESSONS.md exists. Trading a few extra cycles on DIV/REM for a much shorter
clock period should improve CoreMark iterations per second substantially.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Give DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU a shared, blocking multicycle execution
unit, leaving the base integer ALU and existing multiplication datapaths
on their current single-cycle path. Remove all synthesizable / and %
logic from the core's instantiated ALU. The divider captures the actual
forwarded source values once and computes unsigned magnitudes using
four explicitly unrolled restoring binary division steps per clock,
with quotient and remainder registered between groups. Eight groups
produce all 32 quotient bits. Capture operand magnitudes and sign flags
on the launch edge, and apply sign correction to the eighth group's
output when registering the completed result; do not add separate
preparation or sign-correction states. This is four binary steps per
cycle, not a large
table of trial multiples. Share the quotient/remainder state across all
four operations, use a widened trial remainder and subtraction borrow
to choose each quotient bit, and register the completed signed result
before it enters the normal EX/MEM result and bypass network.

Hold the divide instruction and younger work while the unit is busy,
but let older EX/MEM and MEM/WB instructions drain. Emit an invalid
EX/MEM bubble once the older instruction advances; never retain and
reissue an older store merely because the divider is busy. Keep data
bus stalls distinct from divider stalls, preserve older WB values needed
by a held instruction, suppress redirects from invalid entries, and
accept the divider result into EX/MEM exactly once when MEM can advance.
Hold a completed result stable until accepted, without restarting the
operation or retiring it twice. Resume normal EX/MEM forwarding for a
dependent ALU instruction, branch, load, store, or subsequent divide.

Preserve RV32M signed truncation toward zero, the dividend's remainder
sign, divide-by-zero results, and INT_MIN/-1 overflow behavior. Maintain
the exact existing RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS formulas in the division unit
through the same start/busy/result-accept protocol; do not introduce
assumptions or edit formal depths. The existing liveness check triggers
at cycle 10 and requires the next retirement by cycle 20. Budget at most
ten cycles between adjacent retirements on ready buses, including
consecutive dependent divides and a divide after a taken branch or load.
Release ID/EX on the result-transfer edge so the following instruction
can use the completed EX/MEM result immediately; avoid a rearming bubble.
Retain every arithmetic vector and
migrate DIV/REM tests to the real sequential unit rather than skipping
them. Verify standalone arithmetic and pipeline behavior, then let the
unchanged formal, cosim, CoreMark CRC/marker, and Gowin evaluation gates
determine correctness and fitness. Keep nret=1 and the full external IO
and RVFI contract unchanged. This hypothesis is solely the structural
separation and time sharing of division, with no predictor, cache, or
unrelated multiplication redesign.

title: Fetch-stage bimodal prediction with direct branch targets
motivation:
This core has no registered IF/ID stage: the instruction at the fetch PC
is decoded directly into ID/EX. Nevertheless, every taken conditional
branch and every JAL/JALR currently redirects in EX and discards the
younger fetch, even when the destination is predictable. CoreMark's
repeated loops and direct calls provide opportunities to eliminate
these bubbles under the same approximately 22% instruction/data stalls.
The only recorded experiment is the baseline; there are no previous
predictor attempts or LESSONS.md entries. Its 199.837 ns worst path runs
through forwarding and the combinational M-extension ALU, so a small
fetch predictor has plausible timing headroom, although routing must
still be measured with Gowin.

A read-only run of the existing CoreMark ELF through the unmodified
reference ISS counted 2,922,015 instructions between its MMIO markers,
including 529,588 conditional branches (294,425 taken), 49,367 JALs,
and 13,735 JALRs, with no traps or out-of-bounds accesses. A sequential
two-bit direction model with 64 entries produced 51,857 conditional
next-PC misses, versus 111,175 direction misses for static backward-taken
prediction. Removing direct-JAL corrections as well gives 291,935 net
corrections saved. Against the recorded 4,491,485 baseline cycles,
a one-cycle-per-correction model projects 6.95% throughput improvement
at unchanged Fmax. This is an estimate, not an RTL/stall simulation or
timing result. A 256-entry model only raised that estimate to 7.15%,
so the smaller 64-entry table is the proposed implementation.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one lightweight fetch-stage bimodal predictor: 64 PC-indexed
two-bit saturating direction counters, indexed by PC[7:2], reset to
weakly not taken (01). Use the counter MSB only for positively validated
conditional BRANCH encodings (funct3 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 7). Generate the
predicted target directly as fetch PC plus the sign-extended B immediate.
Predict legal direct JAL unconditionally using its J immediate. Keep
JALR and all other instructions sequential. Do not add a BTB, global
history, return stack, instruction cache, or extra pipeline stage.
This costs 128 direction bits plus prediction metadata and a direct
target adder, without cached targets or tag comparators. Direction-table
aliasing can affect accuracy but cannot supply a stale target.

Carry the exact predicted next PC through the combinational IF/ID bundle
and the existing ID/EX register. Advance the fetch PC to that value only
when the fetched instruction is actually accepted: memory is ready,
load-use/data-memory holds are absent, and no correction flush is active.
Preserve existing bubble behavior when imem is not ready. Predictions
must never flush the branch itself or invalidate its fetched successor.

In EX, derive the architectural next PC from the existing forwarded
branch comparison, JAL/JALR target calculation, and misalignment-trap
rules. Redirect and flush the younger instruction only when this actual
next PC differs from the carried prediction. Perform this comparison
for every valid instruction, including fall-through/non-control/trapping
instructions, so recovery never depends on predictor state being right.
A predicted-taken branch resolving not taken redirects to its own PC+4;
a correct prediction causes no flush. Never speculate to a misaligned
B/J target or outside instruction RAM [0x00000000, 0x00100000): use
sequential prediction and let EX retain the existing architectural
target, trap, and link-write suppression semantics. This prevents
predicted-taken/not-taken errors from creating out-of-bounds speculative
instruction-memory requests.

Qualify correction and predictor training with ID/EX valid and EX
advance (!stall_ex_mem), so a branch held behind an older stalled memory
operation is neither trained repeatedly nor allowed to consume a
speculative successor before resolution can advance. An accepted EX
correction overrides an instruction-memory stall or fetch/load-use
hold. Update one counter per advancing legal conditional branch using
its resolved outcome; saturate at 00/11 and do not train invalid bubbles
or trapping branches. Read-before-write prediction at a same-index
lookup/update is sufficient; the carried predicted PC is authoritative.

Preserve the existing EX/MEM and MEM/WB retirement behavior, forwarded
operands, actual RVFI pc_next, trap discipline, memory-port gating, and
nret=1 interface. Check direction reversals, cold and aliased counters,
correctly predicted self-loops/direct jumps, unpredicted JALR, and
corrections coincident with both bus stalls. The expected gain is fewer
cycles between the unchanged CoreMark MMIO markers; acceptance still
requires canonical CRCs, formal/cosim correctness, and median Gowin
Fmax times measured iterations/cycle exceeding 12.12 by more than 4.6%.

title: Remove redirect feedback from early divider operand preparation
motivation:
The current champion scores 82.05 iter/sec at a median 36.852 MHz.
Both it and the baseline record 4,491,485 measured CoreMark cycles;
improving global clock timing has delivered the champion's gain.
Its reported worst path takes 34.618 ns and 56 cells, starting at
cpu/u_ex/reg_q.rd_1_s0 and ending at cpu/u_ex/u_div/quotient_q_14_s1
through execute, fetch and the register file. This is consistent with
forwarded branch resolution driving redirect, redirect replacing the
fetched instruction with a NOP, the replacement changing register-file
read addresses, and the early divider launch forming signed operand
magnitudes from those reads. The current RTL also uses early_start,
which includes decode validity and memory readiness, to select the
divider's operand and operation buses before magnitude arithmetic.
Thus a control decision can traverse operand selection and negation
before reaching divider state. No LESSONS.md exists. The previous
micro_opt attempt kept division fully combinational and reached only
13.01 iter/sec; this proposal instead shortens the champion's newly
exposed launch path without changing its sequential arithmetic schedule.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Isolate early divider operand preparation from redirect and launch
qualification. Keep the existing four-restoring-steps-per-clock,
eight-clock divider, early launch opportunity, pipeline stages and
instruction-cycle counts. This is one local control/data-path timing
optimization, not a new divider algorithm or pipeline stage.

In IF, expose the raw imem_data instruction to combinational decode
and register-file read addresses even during a redirect or unready
fetch. Suppress acceptance solely with the existing valid bit and
flush controls. Add explicit fetch-valid qualification to load-use
detection so inactive raw instructions cannot create an interlock.
In ID, retain the raw combinational decoded view, including operands
and operation, but capture an all-zero ID/EX bubble on an invalid
fetch when the register can advance. Preserve reset/flush priority
and all stall holds. In particular, invalid raw instructions must
never leave residual reg_write, rd or memory controls in pipeline
registers: MEM/WB intentionally retains forwarding metadata during
a data stall and its forwarding qualification is not simply valid.

In EX, select the candidate divider operation, operand buses and
metadata source using the registered ID/EX occupancy, !in.valid,
rather than early_start. Whenever EX is empty, continuously prepare
the raw decode candidate and its existing EX/MEM-to-decode bypassed
operands, independently of redirect, decoded.valid and stall. When
EX is occupied, use its existing forwarded operands. Keep early_start
and div_start as separately qualified capture enables: early launch
still requires a valid DIV/REM decode, an empty EX slot, an idle unit,
no pending result and ready MEM. Normal EX launch, divider_wait,
captured RVFI operands, metadata capture and result acceptance retain
their current protocol. Ungranted operand computations have no side
effects. Do not qualify candidate operation or data with fetch-valid;
qualification belongs on the capture enable, not before negation.

This removes both instruction-to-NOP address switching and
early_start-controlled wide operand multiplexing from the signed
magnitude path. Redirect may still qualify a register enable, but
should no longer feed a register-file read and then a 32-bit negate
on its way to divider state. CoreMark cycles between the unchanged
MMIO markers should remain identical for the same bus-ready sequence,
making any accepted gain come from median Gowin Fmax. A 20% fitness
gain would require roughly 44.2 MHz at unchanged cycles; this is an
estimate, not a measured result. The main risk is another path,
including the existing four-step divider recurrence, becoming limiting.

Preserve nret=1, every external memory/RVFI port, decoder default
illegality and all ALTOPS and real RV32M arithmetic. Check unaccepted
fetches carrying legal DIV/REM during imem stalls and branch flushes, wrong-path
memory operations, zero destinations, load-to-divide bypassing,
branch/load bubbles and completion under dmem backpressure. Require
unchanged bounded-progress behavior and no wrong-path divide launch,
false forwarding, duplicate retirement or repeated memory side effect.
Validate with the existing arithmetic suite, formal and cosim gates,
canonical CoreMark CRC/marker checks and median vendor timing; do not
weaken checks or change any evaluation-contract file.

changes.description:
Drive out.instr directly from imem_data rather than replacing it
with NOP on flush/redirect. Preserve out.valid suppression and
redirect-over-stall PC update priority. Update comments to describe
validity-based suppression and raw combinational decode.

Keep the decoded combinational view and regfile addresses raw and
independent of fetch-valid. When advancing ID/EX with in.valid=0,
capture the all-zero bubble instead of the raw decoded payload.
Preserve reset/flush priority, valid decode capture and stall holds.

Add an if_id_valid input and qualify load_use_hazard with it so
invalid raw instruction bits cannot interlock fetch or decode.
Preserve redirect, bus-stall and divider-wait priorities.

Connect if_id_w.valid to the hazard unit's new qualification input
without changing top-level ports, RVFI routing or retirement width.

Select divider candidate operation, source operands and metadata
using registered EX occupancy instead of early_start. Prepare raw
decode operands with the existing early memory bypass whenever EX
is empty. Keep launch/metadata-capture enables fully qualified and
retain divider wait, completion, acceptance and EX/MEM bubble logic.
Eliminate redirect/valid/stall dependencies from candidate data
selection before the divider's magnitude conversion.

Add directed checks for raw invalid fetches containing DIV/REM,
branch-flushed divides and stores, and an invalid fetch whose
register fields match a load destination. Check no false interlock,
launch, forwarding or side effect. Exercise early launches after

title: Retime divider operand preparation behind its launch registers
motivation:
The champion already removed combinational division, raising fitness to
82.05 at a median 36.852 MHz. Its reported worst path is now 34.618 ns
across 56 cells, from EX/MEM rd through execute, fetch redirect gating,
the register file, and into div_unit. The divider currently converts
forwarded operands to unsigned magnitudes on its launch edge, combining
the early-decode bypass/control path with a 32-bit conditional negation.
This is an operand-launch bottleneck rather than evidence that the
whole pipeline needs more stages. The log contains one successful
structural attempt, the existing blocking divider, and no LESSONS.md.
Retiming its preparation arithmetic can raise Fmax without increasing
CoreMark cycles or the bounded retirement gap that formal requires.

edge captures raw forwarded a/b and operation/sign metadata, with no

existing seven groups of four full-width restoring steps and the final
registered sign correction. There must still be exactly eight busy
microcycles after launch, followed by the unchanged result-accept
protocol; do not add a preparation state, rearm bubble, or extra cycle.

title: Tagged cached-target prediction on the multicycle-divider champion
motivation:
The current champion scores 82.05 iter/sec at 36.852 MHz and has no
branch prediction. Every taken branch, JAL, and JALR discards a younger
fetch even though CoreMark repeatedly executes the same control flow.
The prior predictor experiment reduced marker-bracketed cycles from
4,491,485 to 4,201,766, but synthesized the old combinational divider
and reached only 5.370 MHz. That result does not measure prediction on
the current champion. There is no LESSONS.md in this fixture.

The champion's reported critical path crosses EX, IF, the register
file, and early divider launch. Computing B/J targets from fetched
instruction bits and adding a correction-controlled instruction mux
is therefore unattractive. Cached targets can remove recurring control
bubbles without a fetch-data-to-target-adder path. The acceptance
threshold is 85.83 iter/sec, so preserving Fmax is essential.

A read-only reference run of the existing canonical CoreMark ELF
counted 2,922,015 instructions between the markers, including 529,588
conditional branches, 49,367 JALs and 13,735 JALRs, without traps or
out-of-bounds accesses. A sequential 64-entry tagged BTB model using
index PC[7:2] XOR PC[13:8] made 58,584 next-PC errors, versus 357,527
existing taken-control redirects: 298,943 potential corrections saved.
Assuming one cycle saved per correction against the champion's logged
4,491,485 cycles gives 7.13 percent throughput improvement at fixed
Fmax. A 128-entry folded-index model gives only 7.43 percent, so choose
64 entries to reduce lookup and routing cost. This is a retired-trace
estimate with immediate training, not RTL/stall simulation or timing.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one small tagged next-PC predictor to the existing single-retire
pipeline: a 64-entry direct-mapped branch target buffer with a two-bit
saturating conditional direction counter per entry. Index by the six
bits PC[7:2] XOR PC[13:8], compare the remaining full PC identity, and
cache an aligned target plus a conditional/unconditional kind bit.
Learn conditional branches, direct
JAL, and legal JALR targets from EX, including ordinary returns as
last-target JALR predictions. Do not add global history, a return stack,
a cache, or another pipeline stage. Preserve the champion's fast ALU,
bounded multicycle divider, early divide launch, and nret=1 contract.

A valid tag hit predicts the cached target for an unconditional entry
or a conditional entry whose counter MSB is one; otherwise predict
PC+4. Lookup uses the fetch PC and stored state, with no B/J immediate
extraction, target adder, or regfile operand on the prediction path.
Allocate on an advancing legal conditional branch or jump; initialize
replacement counters to 10 for taken and 01 for not taken, then saturate
on subsequent matching conditional outcomes. Cache the architectural
branch target even on a not-taken branch. Refresh a legal JALR target
on each resolved execution. Allocate only aligned targets inside
instruction RAM [0x00000000, 0x00100000), use exact PC matching, and
reset all valid bits. For a compact exact tag, admit only aligned
source PCs inside instruction RAM, require fetch PC[31:20]==0 and
fetch PC[1:0]==0,
and store PC[19:8]. Together with the folded index this identifies
every aligned 32-bit source PC uniquely; no high-bit aliases are
permitted. Store target[19:2] and reconstruct zero upper/low bits.
Target/tag payload arrays need no reset: invalid entries must select
a fully defined sequential PC.
Use inferred distributed memory with asynchronous lookup and a single
synchronous update port; avoid resetting payload arrays into flops.

Carry the actual selected predicted_next_pc with the fetched instruction
through IF/ID and ID/EX. PC prediction takes effect only when that fetch
is accepted, never during imem, load-use, dmem, or divider holds.
At EX compute the architectural next PC with existing forwarded branch
operands, JALR bit-zero clearing, and misalignment/trap fallback. Only
a mismatch against the carried predicted PC redirects and flushes the
younger instruction. Compare for every advancing valid instruction,
including non-control and illegal instructions, because a stale BTB
hit is a performance error rather than permission to change execution.
A mispredicted not-taken branch recovers to its own PC+4; correct
predictions retain the successor. A stale non-control or trapping
prediction must also recover and invalidate its matching BTB entry.
Preserve actual resolved pc_next for RVFI, independently of prediction.

Qualify training and recovery with actual EX acceptance, not just valid:
!stall_ex_mem and no outstanding divider wait. For DIV/REM, perform any
stale-prediction recovery exactly once at result acceptance, using the
prediction captured with that divide; preserve early-launch metadata
and the ready-bus ten-cycle retirement-gap bound. Held branches must
not repeatedly train. Recovery overrides an imem or load-use hold;
an older stalled memory operation delays EX acceptance and recovery.
No wrong-path decode may launch a divider or produce a memory effect.
A lookup/update collision may observe old predictor state: the exact
prediction carried by each accepted instruction remains authoritative.

To keep correction off the champion's operand path, pass raw imem_data
to decode even on a flush and kill work through validity and ID/EX
capture control. Remove the correction-controlled NOP mux on the
instruction/address bits. Qualify load-use detection with fetch validity
and qualify early divider launch with accepted, unflushed decode.
In EX, choose the divider's raw decode versus held EX operands/op using
only EX-slot occupancy, not the flush-dependent early_start signal.
Gate the divider's start enable separately with valid decode, no flush,
ready MEM and available divider state. Unaccepted operands can toggle
but must never be captured. This prevents correction from feeding back
through operand selection, regfile data and signed magnitude arithmetic.
Invalid decoded payload may contain raw bits but may never launch,
redirect, write memory, or retire. This is part of predictor integration:
prediction recovery should control state enables, not mux every source
address before register-file reads and magnitude generation.

Expect about seven percent higher fitness from eliminating recurring
control bubbles while preserving the champion's clock rate. The main
risks are direct-mapped conflicts and a new tag/target-read or correction
path lowering Gowin Fmax. Evaluate with unchanged formal, cosim,
canonical CoreMark CRC/marker/UART, and median Gowin timing gates.
The trace estimate needs Fmax above approximately 35.982 MHz to clear
acceptance, allowing only about 2.36 percent clock loss. Acceptance
requires more than 4.6 percent above 82.05, not above the old 12.12
baseline. Add focused predictor and pipeline tests without
changing the decoder's legality policy or any evaluation infrastructure.

title: Halve divider recurrence depth with parallel radix-4 trials
motivation:
The champion scores 98.36 iter/sec at median 44.18 MHz, with 4,491,485
measured CoreMark cycles. Its 27.182 ns, 134-cell worst path runs from
div_unit divisor state to the signed result register. The current
recurrence cascades four full-width restoring subtraction/mux steps
before final sign correction. Removing redirect from operand preparation
exposed this arithmetic bottleneck. The earlier raw-operand retiming
still reached a four-step recurrence and failed to beat the champion.
No LESSONS.md exists. The prior micro_opt radix-4 attempt kept all sixteen
digits in one combinational path and reached only 13.01 iter/sec; applying
radix-4 inside the existing clocked divider addresses a different depth.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace each group of four serial binary restoring steps in div_unit
with two unsigned radix-4 restoring digit steps. Keep precisely eight
busy clocks after accepted launch, four quotient bits per busy clock,
the existing registered signed result, and the identical start/busy/
result-valid/result-accept interface. This is a local arithmetic mapping
optimization of the existing divider, without new pipeline stages or
instruction scheduling changes.

On launch retain exactly the existing 32-bit unsigned operand magnitudes
and sign flags. Prepare and register the 34-bit constant 3D from the
registered divisor during busy group zero, in parallel with that group's
initial four quotient bits. Form 3D as zero-extended D plus its one-bit
left shift. Derive 34-bit D and 2D by wiring. From group one onward, use
registered 3D in both radix-4 digit steps, so its carry chain lies outside
the repeated recurrence. Do not add 3D arithmetic to the signed launch
path or add a constant-preparation cycle. Use explicit widths throughout,
including D above 2^31 and 3D above 2^32.

Implement group zero with a small initial digit path. With zero initial
remainder, consuming the top four magnitude-dividend bits gives a trial
at most 15. If divisor_q[31:4] is nonzero, the first quotient nibble is
zero and the first remainder is quotient_q[31:28]. Otherwise perform
two narrow radix-4 steps with the four-bit divisor, six-bit D/2D/3D
multiples and seven-bit zero-extended trial subtractions. Select digits
in parallel as below. Register Q = {quotient_q[27:0], quotient_nibble}
and R = {28'b0, remainder_nibble} together with full-width 3D. Divisor
zero must use this narrow path, generating quotient nibble 0xf and
preserving the consumed dividend nibble as remainder. The other seven
busy groups use the shared full-width two-digit recurrence.

Each digit step takes 32-bit quotient Q and remainder R, forms the
34-bit trial T = {R, Q[31:30]}, and computes T-D, T-2D and T-3D in
parallel using 35-bit zero-extended subtraction. The top subtraction
bits indicate borrows. Select the largest fitting digit 3, 2, 1 or 0
using mutually exclusive predicates and a shallow masked-OR mux.
Select the corresponding residual and append the two-bit digit to
Q[29:0]. Retain the low 32 bits of the residual, which are sufficient
because R < D for a nonzero divisor and no more than 32 dividend bits
are consumed overall. Compose exactly two such steps per busy clock,
feeding the first residual and shifted quotient into the second.
All three trial subtractors in each step must be independent, rather
than three cascaded subtract-and-test operations. Do not put a separate
full-width magnitude comparator ahead of each subtractor.

Keep quotient/remainder selection and sign correction on the eighth
group's output as today. Division by zero naturally selects digit 3
at every step, producing quotient 0xffffffff and remainder magnitude_a;
retain suppression of quotient negation when b=0 and the dividend's
remainder sign. Preserve INT_MIN/-1, signed truncation toward zero,
mixed signs, unsigned high-bit operands and all x0 behavior. Leave the
exact four RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS formulas and their eight-cycle protocol
unchanged; the new recurrence belongs only to the real-arithmetic
branch. Preserve early decode launch, memory backpressure, one-time
operand/metadata capture, stable unaccepted results and simultaneous
accept/start behavior without changes to EX or hazard handling.

The intended benefit is two serial trial-selection stages instead of
four at unchanged CoreMark cycles. A 20% fitness improvement would
require approximately 53 MHz; this is an estimate, not a measurement.
Added parallel subtractors and 3D state trade modest area for shorter
depth. Main risks are routing of the parallel subtractors, the group-zero
selection mux, and another core path becoming limiting. Require
median Gowin timing to improve by more than the 4.6% acceptance margin.
Use the existing real-arithmetic, formal, cosim and canonical CoreMark
CRC/marker gates without changing their contracts, formal depth, nret=1,
external ports, decoder defaults or retirement rules.

title: Compute one radix-16 division digit per cycle with registered trial multiples
motivation:
The champion scores 98.36 iter/sec at 44.18 MHz. Its 27.182 ns,
134-cell worst path runs entirely inside u_ex/u_div, from divisor_q
to the signed result register. The current recurrence cascades four
full-width restoring subtract/select steps and final sign correction
in one clock. The prior structural launch-retiming experiment reached
only 43.484 MHz because it retained that arithmetic recurrence.
Moving the launch boundary again therefore does not address the
measured bottleneck. No LESSONS.md exists in this fixture.

The earlier fully combinational radix-4 attempt still cascaded sixteen
digit stages and barely improved the original combinational divider.
This proposal instead changes the recurrence of the already bounded
sequential divider: one quotient digit per clock, with its candidate
differences evaluated in parallel. The existing 3229 LUT4 footprint
leaves room to trade arithmetic replication for less serial depth.

A temporary implementation of this exact recurrence passed the existing
real divider and pipeline cocotb suites, plus added radix-16 boundary
vectors. Gowin builds of the full core with the unchanged timed wrapper
and stall generator reached 46.947, 47.316 and 47.316 MHz for placement
options 0, 1 and 2, respectively: median 47.316 MHz, 7.10 percent above
the champion. Area was 4160 logic LUTs and 869 registers. The reported
worst path moved to forwarding and the ordinary execute ALU. These are
scratch-prototype timing and unit-test results, not a completed formal
or CoreMark fitness evaluation of the future implementation.

hypothesis.motivation:
The champion scores 98.36 iter/sec at 44.18 MHz. Its 27.182 ns,
134-cell worst path runs entirely inside u_ex/u_div, from divisor_q
to the signed result register. The current recurrence cascades four
full-width restoring subtract/select steps and final sign correction
in one clock. The prior structural launch-retiming experiment reached
only 43.484 MHz because it retained that arithmetic recurrence.
Moving the launch boundary again therefore does not address the
measured bottleneck. No LESSONS.md exists in this fixture.

The earlier fully combinational radix-4 attempt still cascaded sixteen
digit stages and barely improved the original combinational divider.
This proposal instead changes the recurrence of the already bounded
sequential divider: one quotient digit per clock, with its candidate
differences evaluated in parallel. The existing 3229 LUT4 footprint
leaves room to trade arithmetic replication for less serial depth.

A temporary implementation of this exact recurrence passed the existing
real divider and pipeline cocotb suites, plus added radix-16 boundary
vectors. Gowin builds of the full core with the unchanged timed wrapper
and stall generator reached 46.947, 47.316 and 47.316 MHz for placement
options 0, 1 and 2, respectively: median 47.316 MHz, 7.10 percent above
the champion. Area was 4160 logic LUTs and 869 registers. The reported
worst path moved to forwarding and the ordinary execute ALU. These are
scratch-prototype timing and unit-test results, not a completed formal
or CoreMark fitness evaluation of the future implementation.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the four cascaded binary restoring steps per busy cycle with
a shared radix-16 restoring datapath. Produce four quotient bits per
clock for the same eight busy cycles, keeping the existing div_unit
start/busy/result_valid/result_accept interface, operand-magnitude
capture on launch, early decode launch, and registered completion.
All DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU operations share this quotient/remainder state.

Capture the 32-bit dividend and divisor magnitudes and sign flags on
the accepted launch edge exactly as today. During busy group zero,
register zero-extended divisor multiples M[k] = k*D for k=1..15 at
36-bit width. Use shifts and explicit add/subtract expressions for
the odd multiples, and shifts of those for the even multiples; do
not infer general multipliers or calculate multiples on the launch
path or within the recurring digit feedback path. These registers
remain constant throughout the following seven busy cycles.
A concrete tested construction is M[1]=D, M[3]=(D<<1)+D,
M[5]=(D<<2)+D, M[7]=(D<<3)-D, M[9]=(D<<3)+D,
M[11]=(D<<3)+M[3], M[13]=(D<<4)-M[3], and M[15]=(D<<4)-D;
each even M[k] is M[k/2]<<1. All operands and intermediate shifts
in these expressions are explicitly 36 bits. Reset the multiple
registers deterministically and update them only in busy group zero.

Calculate the first quotient nibble concurrently with that multiple
preparation, without adding a preparation cycle. The first trial
consists only of dividend_magnitude[31:28] and is at most 15. If
divisor_magnitude[31:4] is nonzero, this nibble is zero and the
remainder is the trial. Otherwise use four narrow restoring steps
with a five-bit subtraction and the four-bit divisor. Assemble
quotient = {dividend_magnitude[27:0], first_quotient_nibble} and
remainder = zero-extended first_remainder. A zero divisor takes the
narrow path and generates nibble 15 while retaining the trial.

For groups one through seven, form the 36-bit trial
T = {remainder_q, quotient_q[31:28]}. Compute all fifteen
differences {1'b0,T} - {1'b0,M[k]} in parallel at 37-bit width.
Each difference's top bit is its borrow; derive the fit flag from
that same subtraction instead of serial compare-then-subtract logic.
Select the largest fitting k, or zero when none fits, and select its
difference as the next remainder; k=0 selects T. Use mutually
exclusive masks and a balanced OR reduction for the remainder and
digit outputs, avoiding a fifteen-level priority mux chain. For
ordered multiples, selected[k] = fits[k] && !fits[k+1] for k=1..14,
selected[15] = fits[15], and selected[0] = !fits[1]. Append the chosen
nibble with quotient_next = {quotient_q[27:0], digit}. Explicitly
retain full widths until selection, then register remainder[31:0];
the selected remainder fits 32 bits for every legal operand pair.
For D=0, all candidates fit, digit 15 is selected and the remainder
accumulates the original dividend, preserving RV32M zero-divisor
behavior without a long exceptional-case datapath.

Apply the existing quotient/remainder sign correction when registering
the eighth group's selected result. Preserve truncation toward zero,
the dividend's remainder sign, the non-negated all-ones zero-divisor
quotient, and INT_MIN/-1 wraparound. Keep every RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS
formula exact and its eight-cycle control schedule identical to real
arithmetic. Keep result stability while acceptance is delayed, reset
cancellation, and simultaneous acceptance/new launch behavior.
The existing early-launch and pipeline interlocks need no topology
changes; preserve the ten-cycle ready-bus retirement-gap bound, exact
RVFI operands, channel-0 retirement, and nret=1.

This is one structural replacement of the divider recurrence. The
intended benefit is one full-width parallel subtract/select level
followed by sign correction, instead of four serial subtract/select
levels followed by sign correction, with unchanged instruction cycle
counts. At equal cycles, acceptance requires median Fmax greater
than 46.213 MHz, corresponding to more than 102.885 iter/sec. Expect
roughly seven percent higher fitness, approximately 105.34 iter/sec,
if the final implementation reproduces the measured scratch timing
and the champion's marker-bracketed cycle count. The ordinary execute
path now limits the prototype, so the original theoretical divider
speedup does not translate into a comparably large whole-core gain.
The remaining uncertainty is implementation-dependent mapping and
routing of the replicated subtractors and whether the full unchanged
correctness/fitness gates confirm the estimate. Assess gains with real
arithmetic tests, formal/cosim, CoreMark CRC/marker/UART gates, and
median Gowin timing rather than a LUT-depth estimate alone.

title: Timing-isolated bimodal prediction with one-bit EX recovery
motivation:
The champion scores 98.36 iter/sec at 44.18 MHz and takes 4,491,485
marker-bracketed CoreMark cycles. Every taken conditional branch and
direct jump currently discards the younger fetch. The first predictor
attempt reduced cycles to 4,201,766 but used the obsolete combinational
divider. The later tagged-target predictor reached 4,192,580 cycles
but only 39.69 MHz and 94.67 iter/sec; its worst path crossed EX,
predictor, IF, decode and early divider launch. There is no LESSONS.md.
Prediction needs to preserve the current champion's clock rate rather
than repeat that large cached-target and recovery path. A small
instruction-qualified direction predictor can remove most of these
bubbles without target tags, stored targets or a 32-bit recovery compare.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 64-entry, two-bit bimodal conditional direction predictor indexed
by fetch PC[7:2], plus unconditional prediction of legal direct JAL.
Reset the counters to weakly not taken. Use two explicit banks of
64 clocked bits, with asynchronous indexed reads and synchronous
updates; do not forward the current EX update into the fetch lookup.
Read the old indexed counter for saturating training, not a carried
stale counter snapshot. Only advancing, valid, legal conditional
branches update the table, at most once each. Direction aliasing is
allowed, but the current fetched instruction supplies the target.
There is no BTB, target memory, tag compare, global history or RAS.

Positively predecode legal BRANCH funct3 values and direct JAL from
raw imem_data. Form the B/J immediate and share one fetch PC-relative
target adder. A branch predicts a transfer only when its counter MSB
is one; JAL predicts a transfer unconditionally. Admit predictions
only for word-aligned source and target addresses in instruction RAM
[0x00000000, 0x00100000). Otherwise predict PC+4 and let ordinary EX
handling preserve architectural control flow and misalignment traps.
Keep JALR sequential and resolve it through the existing EX path.
Update the PC only when fetch really advances; holds never consume
a prediction, and an accepted correction overrides imem backpressure.

Carry only a predicted_transfer bit with each accepted instruction
through IF/ID and ID/EX. Because prediction is qualified by the
actual instruction and uses its exact B/J immediate, EX need not
compare two 32-bit next-PC buses. Derive actual_transfer from the
existing forwarded branch outcome or jump control, suppressed by
the existing target-misalignment fault. Redirect when actual_transfer
XOR predicted_transfer is true, qualified by valid and EX advance.
For an actual transfer recover to the authoritative EX target; for
a predicted transfer resolving to fall-through recover to the
instruction's own PC+4. Correct predictions leave the successor
valid. JALR has predicted_transfer=0 and therefore redirects normally.
Invalid, reserved, arithmetic, memory and DIV/REM instructions never
predict transfers, so they need no stale-BTB recovery. Preserve the
actual resolved pc_next, link value and trap suppression for RVFI.

Keep prediction and correction out of early divider operand and
opcode selection. Continue to decode raw instruction bits on flush;
gate state acceptance rather than muxing source addresses to NOPs.
For the empty-EX early divider launch, supply an imem-ready decode
eligibility independent of correction and fetched predicted direction.
Gate this candidate with registered !ID/EX.valid, a validated divide
opcode, ready MEM, and available divider state. A correcting branch
necessarily occupies EX, so this empty-EX qualifier already prevents
a wrong-path early launch. Normal divide launches likewise depend on
their registered EX entry. Do not feed flush-dependent decoded.valid
into the early launch arithmetic/control cone; its independent
readiness is safe only with the mandatory empty-EX guard. Keep the
existing blocking divider, eight arithmetic groups, early operand
capture, result handshake and ready-bus liveness bound unchanged.

The prior direct-prediction cycle count projects a 6.90 percent
throughput gain at unchanged 44.18 MHz, about 105.1 iter/sec. Clearing
4.6 percent above 98.36 requires more than 102.885 iter/sec, or about
43.23 MHz if that cycle count repeats. This is an estimate, not a new
RTL or Gowin result. The main risk is the fetch target adder or
counter-read mux reducing Fmax by more than roughly two percent.
Preserve nret=1, every IO/RVFI field, decoder legality, all arithmetic
behavior, and all formal/cosim/CoreMark CRC, marker and UART gates.

title: Register forwarding decisions from pipeline next-state tags
motivation:
The champion scores 107.83 iter/sec at 48.433 MHz with 4,491,485
marker-bracketed CoreMark cycles. The recent radix-4 micro_opt improved
fitness by 9.63 percent and exposed a different bottleneck: forwarding
through the ordinary execute ALU to data memory. The radix-16 candidate
also exposed that path and scored only 105.02. No LESSONS.md exists.
A fresh unchanged-core Gowin placement reproduces 48.303 MHz and the
25.997 ns path. Its cell detail shows WB destination-tag comparison,
operand selection, a DSP multiplication and result selection in series.
Retiming the small forwarding decisions can remove tag comparison from
this arithmetic path without adding a pipeline stage or instruction cycle.
A scratch prototype of this exact next-state retiming passed all 18
existing pipeline tests. Gowin placements 0/1/2 reached 53.390, 57.457
and 57.457 MHz, giving a 57.457 MHz median. Placement-zero area was
3430 LUT4s and 638 FFs versus the champion's 3468 LUT4s and 634 FFs;
DSP count remained six. These are prototype timing and unit-test results,
not a completed formal/cosim/CoreMark fitness evaluation.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Register the two existing two-bit EX forwarding selectors on the same
edge as the pipeline entries they describe. Compute each selector from
the exact next-state source tags and next-state producer tags/control,
rather than comparing the current registered tags combinationally in EX.
Keep the current NONE/EX_MEM/MEM_WB encoding and EX_MEM-over-MEM_WB
priority. This is one local control-retiming optimization: the operand
muxes, ALU, multiplier, divider and all instruction latencies remain as
they are. There is no predictor, cache, wider issue or new execution stage.

Express the existing ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB register updates as
combinational next-state bundles followed by their original clocked
capture. Preserve the complete reset, hold, flush, divider-completion,
bubble and trap priorities exactly. Expose the relevant next-state tags
and controls internally to the forwarding unit; exposing whole typed
next-state bundles is also acceptable, with only needed fields consumed.
ID/EX next state supplies rs1_addr and rs2_addr. EX/MEM next state supplies
rd and valid && ctrl.reg_write. MEM/WB next state supplies rd and
ctrl.reg_write with precisely the existing qualification.

Use these next-state values to compute fwd_rs1_next and fwd_rs2_next
with the current priority and nonzero-destination rules. Clock the
selectors alongside the pipeline captures and reset both to NONE.
After every edge, each registered selector must equal what the original
combinational forward_unit would have computed from the resulting
current pipeline registers. Feed these registered selectors into the
existing EX operand muxes. No forwarding decision arrives a cycle late:
consumer and producer next states and their matching selectors are
captured together. Keep raw regfile reads and the WB write-first bypass.

This exact next-state approach is essential. Do not merely compare raw
decode addresses against the current ID/EX and EX/MEM destinations and
hold those predictions forever. Data stalls retain ID/EX and EX/MEM
while MEM/WB clears only valid and retains forwarding data. Divider
waits drain older stages; divider acceptance inserts captured metadata
and its destination into EX/MEM. Load-use and redirect flushes insert
zero bubbles, and traps can suppress reg_write. Compute selectors from
those authoritative updates, including simultaneous divide acceptance
and younger-instruction capture, so stall/drain/flush transitions remain
identical to the champion. In particular, do not add MEM/WB.valid to its
forwarding enable: retained data is intentionally usable after retirement
during a data stall. Preserve the separate empty-EX decode bypass and
early divider launch, which do not use these normal EX selectors.

The timing benefit is that EX operand selection starts from selector
flip-flops, removing producer-tag equality, write-enable priority and
selection encoding from the path into DSP multiplication. Next-state
comparisons end at small selector registers and do not include the
full multiplication datapath. Watch the new selector-input paths through
redirect/flush and trap suppression, especially JALR low-bit alignment;
preserve all dependencies rather than relaxing trap behavior. The main
uncertainty is whether those paths or the existing divider then limit
the final implementation's median Fmax. The measured scratch median
projects 127.924 iter/sec at 4,491,485 cycles, approximately 18.64 percent
above the champion. Expect about nineteen percent better fitness if
implementation reproduces the retiming and unchanged instruction cycles.
Placement zero's worst path now begins at WB mem_to_reg control and
crosses the existing DSP datapath; a divider recurrence path is close
behind at 24.001 ns. Producer-tag comparison no longer starts that path.

Acceptance at unchanged cycles requires median Fmax above approximately
50.661 MHz and fitness above 112.790 iter/sec. Confirm with the standard
formal, cosim, real-arithmetic and canonical CoreMark CRC/marker/UART
gates and median Gowin timing. Keep nret=1, every external IO/RVFI field,
decoder default illegality, exact ALTOPS formulas, arithmetic bits,
bounded progress and retirement ordering unchanged.

title: Isolate multiplication in a registered partial-product execution unit
motivation:
The champion scores 107.83 iter/sec at 48.433 MHz with 4,491,485
marker-bracketed CoreMark cycles. Its reported 25.997 ns worst path
now crosses forwarding and u_ex/u_alu. A fresh option-0 Gowin report
reproduces this path and explicitly identifies the combinational
mul_uu DSP between the forwarding mux and the shared result path.
The latest structural radix-16 divider attempt reached only 47.17
MHz and had the same ordinary-execute bottleneck. The current ALU
places three combinational multiply expressions behind operand
forwarding and ahead of the shared EX/MEM result register. Registering
multiplication separately can shorten the common execute path while
charging additional cycles only to multiply instructions. No
LESSONS.md exists; the experiment history contains no multiplication
execution-unit separation attempt.

A scratch prototype of this proposal reached 56.165, 58.837 and
58.837 MHz for Gowin placement options 0, 1 and 2, a median of
58.837 MHz. It used 3585 logic LUTs, 782 registers and two DSPs,
versus the champion's 3468 LUTs, 634 registers and six DSPs.
CoreMark completed with the canonical CRCs, UART validation and
start/stop markers in 4,773,913 cycles under the unchanged random
imem/dmem stalls. The resulting projection is 123.247 iter/sec,
14.30 percent above 107.83 despite 6.29 percent more cycles.
The real multiplier tests, existing pipeline suite with an added
multiply/divide dependency stream, and stalled selftest/random1/
random2/random3 full-trace cosim passed. The unchanged nret=1 fast
formal suite also passed all 53 checks, including liveness, illegal
instructions, retirement uniqueness and every multiplication ALTOPS
routing check. These are scratch-prototype results, not an
orchestrator acceptance of the future implementation.

start/stop markers in 4,773,913 cycles under the unchanged random

14.30 percent above 107.83 despite 6.29 percent more cycles.
The real multiplier tests, existing pipeline suite with an added
multiply/divide dependency stream, and stalled selftest/random1/
random2/random3 full-trace cosim passed. The unchanged nret=1 fast

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move MUL, MULH, MULHU and MULHSU out of the combinational fast ALU
into one blocking, clocked multiplier with registered operands,
registered 16-bit partial products, and a registered final result.
Keep ordinary integer instructions, branches, loads and stores on
the present execute path and keep the existing eight-group radix-4
divider unchanged. This is one structural separation of multiplication,
without a predictor, cache or wholesale pipeline-depth change.

On an accepted launch, capture the actual post-forward a/b values,
multiply operation and the instruction's RVFI metadata exactly once.
Split each captured operand into a 16-bit unsigned low half and a
signed 17-bit upper half. The upper half is sign-extended for a in
MULH/MULHSU, for b in MULH, and zero-extended otherwise. MUL's low
result is independent of signedness, so use unsigned halves for MUL.
In the first busy clock register four parallel products:
p00 = a_lo*b_lo as unsigned 32 bits,
p01 = signed({0,a_lo})*b_hi as signed 33 bits,
p10 = a_hi*signed({0,b_lo}) as signed 33 bits, and
p11 = a_hi*b_hi as signed 34 bits. This shares all four operations
without an operand-magnitude conversion or late sign-negation chain.

In the second busy clock form signed 34-bit cross_term = p01 + p10
+ zero_extended(p00[31:16]). Implement this three-input sum with one
carry-save layer followed by one 34-bit carry-propagate adder:
x and y are sign-extended p01/p10, z is zero-extended p00[31:16],
sum = x XOR y XOR z, carry = ((x AND y) OR (x AND z) OR (y AND z))<<1,
and cross_term = sum + carry, all explicitly 34 bits. Then
low = {cross_term[15:0],p00[15:0]} and
high = p11[31:0] + sign_extended(cross_term[33:16]), modulo 2^32.
Register low for MUL and high for the three high-half operations.
This decomposition follows P = p00 + (p01+p10)*2^16 + p11*2^32
and preserves cross-term carries and signed upper halves exactly.
Use ordinary product expressions and synthesizable registers so
Gowin can infer its DSPs; introduce no vendor-only primitive dependency.
There are exactly two busy clocks after capture and one result-transfer
edge, adding three execute cycles to each multiply in isolation.

Capture forwarded operands before holding ID/EX. While multiplication
is busy, hold fetch and decode but allow older EX/MEM and MEM/WB work
to drain. Insert an invalid EX/MEM bubble once older work advances;
never repeat an older store. A data-memory stall independently holds
the older EX/MEM request. The multiplier may continue internally
during that hold, and a completed result must remain stable until
EX/MEM can accept it exactly once. Release ID/EX on the transfer edge
so the next instruction uses ordinary EX/MEM forwarding without a
rearm cycle. Prevent younger DIV/REM early launches while a multiply
owns EX; consecutive multiply/divide combinations must neither lose
metadata nor restart an operation. Preserve held WB forwarding data.
OR multiplication wait into ex_stage's existing divider_wait output
so the existing core/hazard wiring already supplies the required
fetch/decode hold. Do not add another pipeline stage for ordinary
instructions or a new control path through fetch/decode.
Use mul_start = is_mul && !mul_busy && !mul_valid,
mul_accept = mul_valid && !stall, and
mul_wait = mul_busy || (is_mul && !mul_valid), where stall is the
existing data-memory EX/MEM hold. Capture multiply metadata on
mul_start and select its saved payload with the result on mul_accept.
Keep EX/MEM update priority reset, memory hold, completed arithmetic
result, arithmetic-wait bubble, then ordinary execution. Normal
multiply launch may run behind a held older memory request, but
it must not enable a new launch from the younger decode candidate.

Preserve all four exact RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS multiplication formulas
through the same latency and handshake as real arithmetic. Preserve
every existing real multiplication vector by moving its checks to
the actual sequential multiplier suite, not by deleting or weakening
assertions. Cover signed upper halves, unsigned operands above 2^31,
INT_MIN, negative-by-unsigned MULHSU, low-half wraparound, zero and
x0 destinations, input changes after launch, reset and delayed result
acceptance. Keep nret=1, every external IO/RVFI field, strict retirement
order, legality and memory/trap behavior, and the unchanged formal
liveness depth. Check at most ten cycles between adjacent retirements
on ready buses, including multiply/divide transitions.

The intended gain is a shorter forwarding-to-fast-ALU path and
isolated DSP timing between local registers. Expect fourteen percent
higher fitness, with medium confidence because the final control
wiring and physical mapping may differ from the scratch prototype
and the implemented candidate must pass the full unchanged gates.
Account for added MUL cycles explicitly: acceptance requires more
than 112.79 iter/sec; at the measured 4,773,913 cycles this requires
median Fmax greater than 53.845 MHz. The prototype's 58.837 MHz
clears that threshold by roughly nine percent. Validate real
arithmetic and pipeline behavior, then use the
unchanged formal, cosim, CoreMark CRC/marker/UART and median Gowin
fitness gates; no evaluation-contract changes are proposed.

title: Compact registered lookahead prediction without recovery feedback
motivation:
The current champion scores 107.83 iter/sec at 48.433 MHz and takes
4,491,485 marker-bracketed CoreMark cycles. There is no LESSONS.md.
Earlier direct bimodal prediction reduced cycles to 4,201,740, whereas
tagged cached-target prediction reached 4,192,580 but introduced a
long EX/predictor/fetch/decode/divider path. The last bimodal attempt
scored 104.19 at 43.779 MHz on the older divider implementation; the
current champion has since shortened that divider recurrence, and its
reported worst path instead traverses forwarding and multiplication.
Branch prediction remains a roughly seven-percent throughput opportunity,
but must preserve almost all of the current clock rate. Registering
the direction lookup with the fetch PC removes the direction-table
read mux from the current instruction's target-selection path.

A read-only reference-ISS run of the canonical 2K, -O3, ten-iteration
CoreMark program observed 357,527 baseline taken-control corrections
between the markers, with zero traps and no out-of-bounds accesses.
A model of registered lookahead, old-state reads, delayed training
and invalidation on correction produced 70,829 corrections with
32 counters, saving 286,698. With 64 counters it saved 290,053:
twice the state buys only 3,355 additional saved corrections, about
0.08 percent of baseline cycles. Choose 32 entries to reduce clock
load, lookup depth and routing pressure. This is an architectural
trace model, not an RTL simulation with bus stalls or a timing result.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one 32-entry two-bit bimodal branch-direction predictor with a
registered lookahead lookup, plus unconditional direct-JAL prediction.
Keep the current combinational fetch/decode and all pipeline stages.
Index counters by PC[6:2], reset them to weakly not taken, and update
the indexed current counter once per advancing valid legal conditional
branch. Use explicit clocked counter bits, asynchronous lookup into
the lookahead register, and no combinational EX-update bypass.

The fetch PC and its direction prediction must be one transaction.
For the current raw fetched instruction, positively recognize legal
BRANCH funct3 values and JAL, form the exact B/J immediate, and compute
one shared PC-relative target. Select that target for a branch only
when the registered direction is valid and taken; select it for JAL
unconditionally. Otherwise select PC+4. Predict transfers only when
source and target are word aligned and inside instruction RAM
[0x00000000, 0x00100000). Leave JALR sequential. There is no BTB,
stored target, tag comparison, global history or return stack.

On an ordinary accepted fetch edge, update the PC to this selected
normal next PC and simultaneously capture the counter MSB indexed
by that same normal next PC into a direction register, marking it
valid for the new PC. Prepare two small parallel old-state MSB reads:
one at (PC[6:2]+1) modulo 32, and one at
(PC[6:2]+B_or_J_immediate[6:2]) modulo 32. Select between their
outputs with the same admitted predicted_transfer used to choose
the next PC. For admitted aligned transfers these modular indices
exactly match next_PC[6:2]. Do not feed the full-width target adder,
its range check and next-PC mux serially into an indexed table read;
compute both five-bit indices and table reads independently, and
apply the admission/transfer choice only at the final one-bit mux.
This keeps full-width target validation from preceding a counter
read, while adding only a second small combinational MSB read port.
Counter writes and lookahead reads may use old
state on the same edge; this affects accuracy only. Hold both PC and
registered direction during imem, load-use, dmem and divider holds.
On reset or an accepted EX correction, invalidate the registered
direction and predict the first conditional branch at the recovery
PC not taken; direct JAL remains predictable. The next accepted fetch
restores ordinary lookahead validity. Never look up the correction
target on the correction edge: the counter-read address must depend
only on the normal sequential/predicted fetch successor, not on EX
redirect_target. This deliberately keeps EX recovery arithmetic
out of the table-read-to-register path without adding a fetch bubble.

Carry only a predicted_transfer bit through if_id_t and id_ex_t.
Because a predicted target always comes from the current instruction's
exact immediate, EX recovery needs only actual_transfer XOR
predicted_transfer. Derive actual_transfer from the existing forwarded
branch outcome and jump control, suppressing transfer on the existing
misalignment fault. A direction mismatch redirects to the actual
target when taken, or to the resolving instruction's own PC+4 when
falling through. Qualify recovery and training with valid EX advance,
suppress repeated updates while an older data access holds EX, and
retain correction-over-fetch-hold priority. Correct predictions must
preserve the already fetched successor. Keep actual resolved pc_next,
link values, operand forwarding and trap behavior authoritative for
RVFI; neither prediction nor invalid direction state changes retirement.

Keep correction and prediction out of early divider operand and opcode
selection. Preserve raw instruction decode on flush and gate register
acceptance. Supply imem-ready raw decode eligibility separately from
flush-qualified pipeline validity; early launch requires registered
empty EX, a validated DIV/REM, ready MEM and an available divider.
An EX correction necessarily occupies EX, so the mandatory empty-EX
guard prevents a wrong-path early divide launch. Select candidate
operands by registered EX occupancy alone. Preserve the current
divider arithmetic, launch latency, result protocol and liveness bound.

Subtracting the trace model's 286,698 saved one-cycle corrections from
4,491,485 cycles projects 4,204,787 cycles, a 6.82 percent throughput
gain at constant Fmax. The earlier asynchronous predictor's RTL run
was about 2,190 cycles above its corresponding trace projection;
applying that small discrepancy provisionally gives about 4.207
million cycles and 115.1 iter/sec at 48.433 MHz. Exceeding 107.83 by
4.6 percent requires about 112.79 iter/sec and roughly 47.45 MHz,
allowing only about two percent clock loss. These are estimates;
stall phase, stale direction during holds and placed routing require
measurement. The experiment tests whether registered small-table
lookup can preserve this margin. Expect roughly seven percent higher
fitness, with medium confidence. Preserve
nret=1, the entire IO/RVFI contract, decoder legality, arithmetic and
every unchanged formal, cosim, CoreMark CRC/marker/UART and Gowin gate.

title: Register one-hot forwarding masks alongside pipeline next state
motivation:
The champion scores 125.68 iterations/sec at median 60.0 MHz with
4,773,913 marker-bracketed CoreMark cycles. Its worst option-zero path
starts at EX/MEM rd, traverses forwarding and the fast integer ALU,
and reaches the memory interface in 22.864 ns. Multiplication is now
isolated in its registered unit. No LESSONS.md exists. The earlier
micro_opt hypothesis hyp-20261004-001-r4s0 registered binary forwarding
selectors on the preceding core and reached 55.216 MHz; the current
champion changed the datapath afterward. Registering fully decoded
one-hot masks now removes both tag comparison and binary-selection
decoding from the remaining fast execute path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Retiming the existing forwarding decision into six one-hot mask bits
should shorten the EX operand-to-result path without changing a single
instruction's execution latency. For each source, register a three-bit
NONE/EX_MEM/MEM_WB mask on the same edge as the consumer and producer
pipeline entries it describes. Use NONE=3'b001, EX_MEM=3'b010 and
MEM_WB=3'b100. Compute the mask from exact pipeline next-state tags and
controls, retaining EX_MEM-over-MEM_WB priority and nonzero producer
destinations. In EX, select rs1 and rs2 with the bitwise OR of three
individually masked 32-bit candidates, rather than a binary selector
case. Reset both masks to NONE. This is one forwarding-control mapping
and retiming optimization; keep ALU arithmetic, branch resolution,
multiplier/divider units and schedules, pipeline depth and fetch policy
unchanged.

Express the existing ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB register updates as
authoritative combinational next-state bundles followed by clocked
capture. Preserve every reset, flush, hold, arithmetic-completion,
bubble and trap priority exactly. Expose these next-state bundles
internally to the forwarding unit. ID/EX next state supplies source
addresses; EX/MEM next state supplies rd and valid && ctrl.reg_write;
MEM/WB next state supplies rd and ctrl.reg_write. Compute and register
the one-hot masks from those fields. After each edge, the chosen source
must equal the original combinational forwarding decision for the
resulting pipeline state. Do not derive masks from an assumed normal
pipeline advance or simply hold an old selection throughout arithmetic
waits.

MEM/WB forwarding intentionally uses ctrl.reg_write without valid:
during a data-memory stall it clears valid but retains its previous
result, destination and control for a held dependent EX instruction.
Preserve that qualification exactly. A memory hold, load-use bubble,
redirect flush, mul/div drain, captured arithmetic result acceptance,
misalignment trap and simultaneous younger decode capture must all be
reflected in the same next-state computation that updates the pipeline.
Keep the independent EX/MEM-to-decode bypass and early divide launch
unchanged; those paths do not use the normal EX forwarding masks.

A scratch implementation of this exact one-hot next-state design was
built with the unchanged vendor flow and single-retire FPGA wrapper.
Gowin Fmax was 58.450, 63.060 and 63.060 MHz for placement options
0, 1 and 2: median 63.060 MHz, 5.10 percent above the champion's 60 MHz.
Option zero used 3,639 logic cells and 754 registers, versus the
champion's 3,627 and 748; LUT-RAM, BSRAM and DSP counts were unchanged.
The existing pipeline cocotb suite passed. CoreMark with both random
bus stalls retained exactly 4,773,913 marker-bracketed cycles, reported
all five canonical CRCs and the required validation literal, reached
EBREAK and reported no out-of-bounds access. Combining the measured
scratch median with those cycles yields 132.0929 iterations/sec,
about 5.10 percent above 125.68 and above the 131.46128 acceptance
threshold. These are scratch measurements, not an orchestrator result;
the complete formal and cosim gates still apply to the implementation.

Implement the fully qualified registered one-hot decisions, rather
than registering only tag equality and applying enables later. That
alternative had worse option-zero timing in a separate scratch probe.
The winning scratch implementation's median-placement worst paths
moved into the existing divider recurrence; option zero also exposed
a WB-to-selector path through redirect/flush next-state control. Those
paths limit headroom, and the measured gain has only a small margin
above 4.6 percent, so confidence is medium. Preserve nret=1, all memory
and RVFI ports, decoder default illegality, arithmetic bits and ALTOPS,
trap behavior, bounded progress, strict retirement order and arbitrary
bus backpressure. Change no evaluation-contract file or check.

title: Register fully forwarded operands at the decode-to-execute boundary
motivation:
The champion reaches 125.68 iterations/second at 60 MHz, with
4,773,913 marker-bracketed cycles. Its worst path starts at an EX/MEM
destination tag and traverses forwarding, operand selection and the
ordinary ALU. The structural attempts already isolated division and
multiplication; another arithmetic-unit redesign would miss this
remaining path. The earlier registered-forwarding-selector experiment
improved its parent but left a WB-result mux before the execute datapath.
Resolving complete operand values before their capture should remove
both tag selection and source muxes from the beginning of fast execute.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move the forwarding boundary from the beginning of EX to the input of
the existing ID/EX operand registers. Keep the pipeline depth and the
blocking registered multiply/divide units. Every instruction admitted
to ID/EX must capture the architectural rs1 and rs2 values it will use,
after bypassing all older producers. EX then consumes these registered
values directly, without current-stage tag comparisons or a late
EX/MEM-versus-MEM/WB operand mux. This is a structural relocation of
operand acquisition, not merely registering forwarding selectors.

For each decoded source, use newest-producer priority: the current
advancing EX instruction's actual result, the current advancing MEM
instruction's final writeback value, then the existing write-first
register-file output. Keep WB forwarding inside reg_file's existing
same-cycle write bypass; do not add a second WB comparator/data mux.
The EX candidate is the exact result about to enter EX/MEM: ordinary
ALU output, PC+4 for JAL/JALR, or a completed registered multiply/divide
result together with its saved destination and control metadata.
Exclude loads from this EX bypass: their address is not their result.
Retain the existing one-cycle load-use interlock and all bus waits.
The MEM candidate includes correctly extended load data and suppresses
writes on a misaligned access. Consumer capture and early launch remain
blocked by the existing dmem hold when a load response is unready;
do not insert another ready-controlled data mux in the bypass path.
Ignore x0 and invalid/nonwriting/trapping producers. For each source,
form E = ex_wen && ex_rd != 0 && ex_rd == source, then
M = !E && mem_wen && mem_rd != 0 && mem_rd == source, and R = !E && !M.
Resolve with (ex_data & {32{E}}) | (mem_data & {32{M}}) |
(rf_data & {32{R}}). No outer source-zero mux is needed: nonzero
producer tests exclude forwarding to x0 and the register file supplies
zero. Comparisons run in parallel with producer data computation.

Capture the ALU's final input selection at the same ID/EX boundary:
alu_a is PC for AUIPC or resolved rs1 otherwise; alu_b is immediate
or resolved rs2. Keep separately captured architectural rs1/rs2 for
branches, JALR, store data, M-extension inputs and RVFI. EX's fast ALU
reads the captured alu_a/alu_b directly. Hold every operand and its
instruction together during dmem or arithmetic waits, and flush them
together on redirects/load-use bubbles. An admitted instruction's
operands are already final, so do not reread a vanished WB producer
after a stall or clear values merely because the producer retired.

Expose an EX result candidate whose arithmetic data and destination
selection depend on registered EX occupancy and arithmetic completion,
not on younger decoded operands or fetch eligibility. In particular,
early_start must not feed this candidate or create a combinational
loop through decoded -> early divide -> candidate -> decoded. An
empty-EX early divider still launches from correctly resolved decode
operands with a ready older MEM instruction and the existing guards.
A completing divide/multiply must bypass its captured result to the
next instruction on the same transfer edge, then release ID/EX once.
Preserve drain-versus-hold behavior and exactly-once memory effects.

Prepare the EX candidate exactly as follows. Start with rd = in.rd,
data = in.ctrl.is_jump ? in.pc+4 : alu_result, and enable = in.valid
&& in.ctrl.reg_write && !in.ctrl.mem_read && !in.ctrl.is_illegal
&& !misalign_fault && !is_mul && !is_div. If mul_valid, instead use
mul_result and mul_meta_q.rd, qualified by mul_meta_q.valid and its
reg_write. Otherwise, if div_valid, use div_result and div_meta_q.rd
with the equivalent metadata qualification. Do not use early_start
or stall to select this candidate's data. MEM exposes forward_data
as today and forward_wen = in.valid && ctrl_with_trap.reg_write
&& !ctrl_with_trap.is_illegal. Once decode operands are resolved,
remove ex_stage's redundant early_mem comparison/data mux: select
decoded.rs1_val/rs2_val when registered EX is empty, otherwise the
registered in.rs1_val/rs2_val. Retain the current decoded.valid,
early_start, arithmetic acceptance and hazard equations unchanged.

This moves the common recurrence to registered ALU inputs -> ALU ->
operand-capture mux -> ID/EX registers. Tag comparisons run beside
the ALU rather than before it; immediate/PC source selection ends
at the operand registers. Instruction cycle counts should remain
unchanged. A temporary prototype of the specified two-candidate
resolver passed Verilator lint and every existing pipeline cocotb
case, including stalled M-extension dependencies and the ten-cycle
ready-bus retirement-gap assertions. The canonical 2K, -O3, ten-run
CoreMark simulation with both stall generators passed all five CRCs,

cycles were exactly 4,773,913. Gowin placement options 0/1/2 measured
61.263/62.887/62.887 MHz, median 62.887 MHz, with 3775 logic cells,
804 registers and two DSPs. Projected fitness is 131.73 iter/sec,
about 4.81 percent above 125.68. The new worst path is inside the
unchanged divider rather than forwarding into the ordinary ALU.

Expect five percent higher fitness with medium confidence. The margin
above the 4.6-percent acceptance threshold is narrow: unchanged cycles
require median Fmax above about 62.76 MHz. Reproduce the specified
bypass structure and measure the actual Gowin median; implementations
with duplicate WB/early-MEM muxes reached only 61.152 MHz. Full formal
and trace cosim remain implementation-stage gates, not claims of this
prototype. The main risks are the ALU-to-operand feedback path, early
divider operand timing and physical routing. Preserve nret=1, all external ports,
RVFI order/operands/traps, decoder default illegality, exact ALTOPS
formulas, real RV32M arithmetic and the unchanged liveness bound.
Use the unchanged formal, cosim, CoreMark CRC/marker/UART and FPGA
evaluation gates.

title: Compact bimodal prediction with word-address target arithmetic
motivation:
The current champion scores 125.68 iter/sec at 60.0 MHz and takes
4,773,913 marker-bracketed CoreMark cycles. There is no LESSONS.md.
The four previous predictor experiments all passed formal and cosim,
but none won its tournament round. They reduced the older core's
4,491,485 cycles to about 4.20 million; their timing paths identify
recovery feedback into divider launch, divider arithmetic, and later
forwarding/multiplication as obstacles. The champion now isolates
multiplication, so that earlier cycle saving is worth retesting with
a smaller predictor whose fetch target arithmetic is explicitly short.
A 32-entry registered-lookahead predictor saved nearly as many cycles
as 64 entries, but added two table reads and lookahead control. Avoid
that state and compute safe direct targets in word-address units.

A new read-only reference-ISS run of the canonical ELF observed
529,588 conditional branches, 294,425 taken, 49,367 JALs and 13,735
JALRs between the markers, with zero traps or out-of-bounds accesses.
A model that predicts from old state and delays training by two
instruction events gives 69,293 next-PC misses with 32 entries,
versus 65,592 with 64. Thus doubling direction state saves only
3,701 additional corrections, about 0.08 percent of champion cycles.
Eight and sixteen entries save 260,407 and 273,363 corrections versus
288,234 with 32. Choose 32 to retain most accuracy with a small lookup.
This is an instruction-trace estimate, not an RTL/stall simulation.
